input.question: how does the texture of things touched by my fingers tips get transmitted to my brain to give me that feeling of the object
input.ground_truth: We have receptors on our body, which are proteins embedded on the surface of cells, responsible for the sensations of touch, of which we will focus on mechanical force, heat transferred, and movement When you touch something, you are establishing a few things 1) the shape and smoothness of the object around the point of contact is determined by how many receptors are being activated at once and where on your finger. 2) the amount of force that you're exerting on an object 3) the amount that your fingers have moved after exerting that much force (tells you have pliable or soft the material is) 4) how much heat the object gives off When you put together the signals, your brain interprets it as some sort of texture.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: how does the texture of things touched by my fingers tips get transmitted to my brain to give me that feeling of the object

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your fingers are like little sensors, like the buttons on a toy.

When you touch something—like a soft teddy bear or a bumpy rock—those sensors on your fingers feel it.

Then, tiny messages (kind of like secret notes) travel up your arm, all the way to your brain through special wires called nerves.

When the messages get to your brain, your brain says, “Oh! That’s soft!” or “Oh! That’s bumpy!”

That’s how you know what you’re touching just by feeling it with your fingers!
